To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mice that present higher locomotor response after ethanol, methamphetamine or morphines treatment display increased locomotor responses when rechallenged with ethanol or methamine.
individual characteristics to repeated ethanol administration predict locomotor responses to other drugs.

Mice that present higher vs lower locomotor response to repeated treatment with ethanol, methamphetamine or morphinem, display increased or decreased responses to the other drugs, in an asymmetical pattern.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of repeated drug treatment on the behavioral response to a second challenge.
the study of individual differences and their consequences for drug abuse.
the individual differences in response and adaptation to repeated drug administration, and how they may predict locomotor sensitivity to a second drug.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
individual differences in response after a repeated treatment with ethanol, methamphetamine or morphin, may affect the locomotor response after a challenge with another drug.
individual differences to repeated administration of a drug are not necessarily related to individual differences to repeated treatment with other drugs.
individual characteristics to repeated ethanol administration do not predict sensitivity to the behavioral effects of morphine or methamphetamine, and vice versa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the behavioral responses to drugs of abuse may be affected by the previous exposure of an animal to a drug, and this is a function of the individual differences in response.
individual differences in response during repeated drug administration may predict the locomotor response after a second drug challenge.
the behavioral response to repeated drug administration is a complex trait, with individual differences, which may be predictive of behavioral responses to other drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of a drug challenge are dependent on individual differences to previous drug treatment.
the behavioral response to repeated administration and challenge with drugs is not a simple, one-directional process.
individual differences to repeated drug administration may predict locomotion response to a second challenge.
